title: Gospel of Bartholomew

stories.title: 📜 Gospel of Bartholomew
summaryBullets: After the resurrection, Bartholomew asks Jesus to reveal the hidden mysteries of his descent (section 1).
The disciples fear to hear, but Jesus grants Bartholomew alone the boldness to ask (section 1).
Jesus recounts how he descended into Hades to free Adam and the righteous (section 2).
Michael the archangel pleaded for mercy, and Jesus broke open the gates of death (section 2).
Hades trembles at Jesus’ approach, and Beliar warns that their defeat is at hand (section 3).
The gates of Hades open, and Jesus brings out the patriarchs and prophets (section 3).
The angel of vengeance rends the Temple veil, signifying access to God (section 3).
The cosmic order shakes at the descent and rising of Christ (section 3).
Jesus reveals that daily many souls ascend, though only some enter Abraham’s bosom (section 4).
He receives their offerings as a sacrifice in paradise (section 4).
Christ sits in glory and accepts the praises of the redeemed (section 4).
Bartholomew marvels at the mystery of salvation and sacrifice (section 4).
The apostles ask Mary to recount the Annunciation and Incarnation (section 5).
Mary prays a hymn; cosmic trembling and a great sign appear (section 5).
Jesus manifests in light and reorders reality after her prayer (section 5).
Mary’s testimony confirms the mystery of the Word becoming flesh (section 5).
Bartholomew invokes Christ’s power and confronts Beliar, who is forced to appear (section 6).
Beliar confesses his rebellion, his dominion over demons, and his dread of Christ (section 6).
Jesus commands that these mysteries be kept from unbelievers (section 6).
The text ends with Bartholomew and the apostles glorifying Christ and blessing the assembly (section 6).
crossRefs: Matthew 10:1-4: The twelve are named and sent out with authority over unclean spirits, and Bartholomew stands in that list with no saying and no scene attached to him anywhere in the Gospels, which is the silence this book fills.
Acts 1:13: Bartholomew is named among those gathered in the upper room after the ascension, the last mention Scripture makes of him.

Jude 1:9: Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, does not dare bring a railing accusation but says only, The Lord rebuke you, a restraint worth setting beside the confrontation this book stages between an apostle and Beliar.
1 Peter 3:18-20: Christ, put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit, went and preached to the spirits in prison, the one sentence the descent narrative here is built out of.
Ephesians 4:8-10: Paul argues that the one who ascended must first have descended into the lower parts of the earth, quoting the psalm about leading captivity captive and giving gifts to men.
2 Corinthians 6:15: Paul asks what agreement Christ has with Belial, the only place the New Testament uses the name this book gives the adversary who is brought up in chains and made to speak.

Luke 1:26-38: Gabriel comes to Mary at Nazareth, tells her the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and she answers, Let it be to me according to your word, which is the account the apostles here press her to retell.

Hebrews 10:11-14: Every priest stands day after day offering the same sacrifices that can never take away sins, while Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and then sat down, set against this book's picture of offerings received day by day in paradise.

translationNotes.note: The name is a patronymic, son of Talmai, not a personal name. Scripture lists him among the twelve at Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:14 and Acts 1:13 and says nothing else about him. Not one word of his is recorded anywhere in the New Testament, which is why a book of his questions had room to grow.

The title the manuscripts actually carry. The book is not a narrative but an interrogation: the apostle asks, Christ answers, then Mary answers, then Beliar is compelled to answer. Ancient lists name a Gospel of Bartholomew twice, in Jerome's prologue to his Commentary on Matthew about AD 398 and in the Gelasian Decree, and neither quotes a word of what it condemns.

The Hebrew word means worthlessness or ruin, and the Old Testament uses it in set phrases for lawless men, as at Deuteronomy 13:13 and Judges 19:22 where they are called sons of Belial. By the intertestamental period it had hardened into a proper name for the adversary. 2 Corinthians 6:15 is the only place the New Testament uses it, in the spelling Beliar.

Chief angel. The word occurs twice in the New Testament, at 1 Thessalonians 4:16 for the voice heard at the coming of the Lord, and at Jude 1:9 for Michael. Scripture names Michael and Gabriel and no other angel; the lists of seven archangels standing before God come from books outside the canon.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִיכָאֵל (mikha'el), who is like God
translationNotes.note: Daniel 10:13 calls him one of the chief princes and Daniel 12:1 has him arise at a time of trouble such as never was. Jude 1:9 has him dispute with the devil over the body of Moses and refuse to bring a railing charge, saying only, The Lord rebuke you. Revelation 12:7 has him and his angels war against the dragon. In this book he pleads for mercy before the descent.

The tradition that Christ went down and brought the righteous dead out. The canonical statements are brief and few: Ephesians 4:8-10 on descending before ascending, 1 Peter 3:18-20 on preaching to the spirits in prison, and 1 Peter 4:6 on the gospel preached to the dead. The gates, the pleading, the trembling and the roll of names brought out belong to this book, not to those verses.

The Greek word is borrowed from Persian and means a walled park or hunting garden of the kind Persian kings kept. The Greek translators of the Old Testament used it for the garden in Genesis 2:8. It appears three times in the New Testament: Luke 23:43 to the thief on the cross, 2 Corinthians 12:4 where Paul is caught up into it, and Revelation 2:7 where the tree of life stands in it.

Where the accepted souls go in this book. Luke 16:22-23 is the only passage that uses the phrase, in the account of the rich man and the beggar Lazarus, where Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side and the rich man is in torment with a great chasm fixed between them. The picture of angels ferrying the soul and of a fixed line between the two states comes from there.

The angel of vengeance tears it in this book. Exodus 26:31-33 has it woven of blue, purple and scarlet with cherubim worked into it, hung to divide the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. Leviticus 16:2 lets the high priest past it one day a year and no oftener. Mark 15:38 has it torn in two from top to bottom at the moment of death, and Hebrews 10:19-20 calls the new way in a road through the curtain.

When Beliar is made to confess his dominion over the demons he is describing a ranked order, and the New Testament uses the same vocabulary. Ephesians 6:12 sets the struggle against principalities, against powers, against the world rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. Colossians 2:15 has Christ disarm them and lead them in a public triumph.

The name is the ordinary Hebrew word for man, and it plays against adamah, the ground he is taken out of. Genesis 2:7 has God form the man from the dust of the ground and breathe into his nostrils the breath of life. Genesis 3:19 turns the same two words into the sentence: dust you are, and to dust you shall return. That pairing is why freeing Adam stands at the centre of every descent narrative.

The standard length measure, the forearm from elbow to fingertip, about eighteen inches. Everything built in Scripture is given in cubits: Genesis 6:15 makes the ark three hundred cubits long, and Deuteronomy 3:11 gives the iron bedstead of Og of Bashan as nine cubits by four. When an ancient text wants to say a thing is enormous it hands the reader a figure in cubits and lets him do the arithmetic.

The book closes with a command that these things not be told to the unworthy. Matthew 10:27 has Jesus command the opposite, that what the disciples hear whispered they are to proclaim from the housetops. Acts 20:20 records Paul insisting he kept back nothing that was profitable and taught publicly and from house to house.

The apostles ask Mary how the conception happened, and she prays first and warns them that fire would come out of her mouth and consume the world if she told it. Luke 1:26-38 gives the annunciation with no such warning attached, and Luke 1:46-55 gives her one recorded song, beginning, My soul magnifies the Lord.

No copy of this book is complete and no two versions agree. Three Greek manuscripts survive, of the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, one of them written into the margins of another book. Two Latin manuscripts survive, and the older of them, Vatican Reg. lat. 1050 of the ninth or tenth century, is the oldest witness in any language. Six Church Slavonic copies survive. They differ in length, in the order of the material, and in what they contain.

Bartholomew is told how many souls leave the world in a day and which of them are received, and Christ is described taking their offerings as a sacrifice. Hebrews 10:11-14 sets the two pictures against each other without leaving room between them: a priest stands day after day offering the same sacrifices which can never take away sins, whereas Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and sat down.

stories.keyTakeaway: An interrogation set after the resurrection. Bartholomew asks what the other disciples are afraid to ask, and the answers make the whole book: the descent and the freeing of Adam, how many souls leave the world each day and which are received, Mary's account of the annunciation given only after she prays, and Beliar dragged up in chains and made to confess his rebellion.

intro:
The Gospel of Bartholomew, which its manuscripts title the Questions of Bartholomew, is set after the resurrection and takes the form of an interrogation. Bartholomew, the apostle listed in Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:14, and Acts 1:13, asks what the other disciples are afraid to ask, and the answers make up the book. The text presented here runs in six sections. Christ tells how he went down and brought Adam and the righteous out; the archangel Michael pleads for mercy; Hades trembles and Beliar warns that their defeat has come; the gates open and the patriarchs and prophets are led out; the angel of vengeance rends the veil of the temple. Bartholomew is then told how many souls ascend each day and which of them are received. The apostles ask Mary to recount the annunciation, and she prays before she will speak. At the end Bartholomew invokes Christ's power and Beliar is brought up in chains and made to confess his rebellion and his dominion over the demons, and the book closes with a command that these things be kept from unbelievers.

No copy is complete and no two versions agree. Three Greek manuscripts survive: Vienna, hist. gr. 67, of the fourteenth century; Jerusalem, Hagiou Saba 13, of the thirteenth, where the text is written in the margins; and Venice, Marciana gr. XI,24, of the fifteenth. Two Latin manuscripts survive: Vatican, Reg. lat. 1050, of the ninth or tenth century, which is the oldest witness in any language, and Rome, Casanatense 1880, of the eleventh. Six Church Slavonic manuscripts survive, the earliest of the fourteenth century and the latest of the eighteenth. They differ in length, in the order of the material, and in what they contain.

A Gospel of Bartholomew is named twice in the ancient lists. Jerome, in the prologue to his Commentary on Matthew, written about AD 398, sets among gospels other than the four one according to Bartholomew, alongside those according to the Egyptians, Thomas, Matthias, the Twelve Apostles, Basilides, and Apelles. The Gelasian Decree, transmitted under the name of Pope Gelasius I (AD 492-496) and dated in its present form to the sixth century, condemns as apocryphal the Gospels in the name of Bartholomew. Neither Jerome nor the Decree quotes a word of what he had in front of him, so neither notice can be tied to the text that survives as the Questions of Bartholomew. A separate work, the Book of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ by Bartholomew the Apostle, survives only in Coptic and is a different book.

No communion receives the Gospel of Bartholomew as canonical.
